listenings.text: Right, this week's book. I'll be honest, I almost didn't read it. I thought it was just another self-help book with a pretty cover. But I'm glad I gave it a chance. The authors went to Okinawa to figure out why so many people there live past a hundred, and the answer isn't a diet or a pill. It's a reason to get up in the morning. The idea I've actually taken up is flow. Every day I try to find one activity where I completely forget the time. For me it's cooking. And the bit that surprised me most? Nobody in the book really retires. They slow down, but they carry on. I found that rather beautiful.

In my research I meet many people who are over ninety, and the first thing I learned is that genes are only a small part of the story. Daily habits matter more. The people who live longest move every day. Not in a gym, usually, but in the garden, on foot, in the house. The second habit is contact with other people. Loneliness is as dangerous for the heart as smoking. And the third is purpose. When patients stop working, I always tell them: please don't just rest. Take up something that gives you a reason to get up. A language, an instrument, a project. The brain needs a purpose as much as the body needs movement.

For forty years I ran a small furniture business in Turin. When I sold it, I thought: finally, I can rest. But after three months I was bored, and a little sad. I missed working with my hands. So at seventy I took up woodcarving. My wife laughed at me. She said, you will give it up in two weeks. That was five years ago. Now I teach a small group of young people every Saturday, in my garage. What keeps me going? Them. They ask me questions, and I have to figure out the answers. I look forward to Saturday all week.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to understand something or find the answer after thinking about it
to do things less quickly; to live at a calmer pace
to start a new hobby or activity
the ability to recover after a difficult time
the reason why you do something, or why your life is important to you
to stop doing something, often because it is difficult
a state when you are so focused that you forget the time

reading.rtitle: Ikigai: A Reason to Get Up in the Morning
paras: On the Japanese island of Okinawa, an unusual number of people live past one hundred. Two Spanish authors, Héctor García and Francesc Miralles, travelled there to figure out why. Their answer is a Japanese word with no direct translation: ikigai, the reason you get up in the morning. For some people it is a family, for others a craft, a garden or a job they love. What matters is that it keeps them going.

The authors noticed that very few people in Okinawa retire in the Western sense. They carry on working, at a slower pace, well into their eighties and nineties. They slow down, but they do not stop. Many of them take up new activities late in life, and they rarely give up the small routines that structure their day: a walk, a garden, a meeting with friends. They also eat simply, and they stop eating before they are completely full.

Two more ideas run through the book. The first is flow: the state in which you are so focused on what you are doing that you forget the time. People who find flow in their daily work tend to be happier. The second is a strong sense of community. Neighbors meet regularly, help each other and share both good news and bad. That network, the authors argue, gives people resilience: when life becomes difficult, they do not face it alone, and they look forward to the next day.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson as a short summary of ideas from Ikigai, by Héctor García and Francesc Miralles

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the summary?
choices: People in Okinawa live longer mainly because of their food.
A clear purpose, active routines, flow and a strong community help people live long and well.
The best way to live longer is to retire early and rest.
